EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

─────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Cross-section “difference-in-differences” (Rajan-Zingales style) supplemented with an instrumental-variables (2SLS) robustness check.  
Rationale  
• We observe two dimensions of exogenous heterogeneity:  
 – across countries in the quality of contract enforcement (RuleOfLaw_c)  
 – across industries in the need for relationship-specific inputs (ContractIntensity_i)  
• The interaction RuleOfLaw_c × ContractIntensity_i is therefore the quasi-experimental “treatment intensity.”  
• Including country and industry fixed effects removes all purely country-level or industry-level determinants, so identification comes only from the differential performance of contract-intensive vs. non-intensive industries inside the same country relative to the same industries in other countries.  
• Because RuleOfLaw may still be endogenous, legal-origin dummies (Brit, French, German, Scandinavian, Socialist) serve as instruments in a 2SLS version of the same specification.  
• A two-year panel (1963 vs. 1997) can be added to create a triple-difference (Country × Industry × Time), but the cross-section alone is sufficient and avoids strong parallel-trend assumptions over 34 years.  

2. Treatment and Control  
• Treatment variable: Treat_ci = RuleOfLaw_c × ContractIntensity_i (continuous).  
• Control group / counterfactual: Country-industry pairs where either  
 (a) the country has weak enforcement (low RuleOfLaw_c) or  
 (b) the industry is not contract-intensive (low ContractIntensity_i).  
• No specific event date or cutoff is needed; identification is cross-sectional.  
(For robustness a binary version—RuleOfLaw above median and ContractIntensity above median—can be used to verify non-linearity.)  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Conditional exogeneity: After country and industry fixed effects plus controls for standard factor endowments, RuleOfLaw_c is uncorrelated with any country-specific comparative-advantage shifters that load differently across industries exactly in proportion to ContractIntensity_i.  
 Plausibility: Relatively strong because each industry’s worldwide average performance is differenced out; remaining concern is omitted variables that vary by (country × industry) in exactly the same pattern—addressed through extensive controls and IV.  
A2. No differential measurement error correlated with RuleOfLaw_c: mis-measurement in ContractIntensity_i (built from U.S. data) is classical.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable; bias likely to attenuate.  
A3. Stable unit treatment value: A country’s judicial quality does not directly change another country’s exports in a way that also depends on that second country’s contract intensity.  
 Plausibility: High—third-country spillovers small relative to own comparative advantage.  
(If a two-period panel is used, add standard parallel-trend assumption for the triple-difference.)  

4. Main Threats and Remedies  
T1. Omitted traditional factor endowments (capital, skill, land) that are correlated with RuleOfLaw_c.  
 Fix: Include interactions of country factor endowments with corresponding industry intensities (capital intensity_i, skill intensity_i, etc.) exactly as in standard HO regressions.  
T2. Reverse causality: A country that specialises in contract-intensive goods may lobby for better courts.  
 Fix: Instrument RuleOfLaw_c with exogenous legal-origin dummies and, in robustness, its 1963 value. Show first-stage F-statistics > 10.  
T3. Global supply shocks or demand shocks that differentially hit contract-intensive industries and also correlate with the geography of good institutions.  
 Fix: Include continent-by-industry fixed effects; run placebo using non-tradable sectors; re-estimate dropping OECD countries.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# -------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high‐dimensional FE and IV
library(modelsummary)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data (assumed .csv in working directory)
trade   <- fread("world_trade_1997.csv")          # country, industry, exports
country <- fread("country_attributes.csv")        # rule_of_law, factor endowments, legal_origin
industry<- fread("industry_attributes.csv")       # contract_intensity, capital_intensity, skill_intensity

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & construct variables
dt <- merge(trade, country,  by = "country_code")
dt <- merge(dt, industry, by = "industry_code")

# Exports: take ln(1+value) to keep zeros
dt[, ln_exports := log1p(exports_usd)]

# Continuous treatment intensity
dt[, treat := rule_of_law * contract_intensity]

# H-O controls
dt[, cap_endow_x_cap_int := cap_per_worker      * capital_intensity]
dt[, skill_endow_x_skill_int := highschool_ratio * skill_intensity]

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3. Baseline DD specification
# ln_exports_ci = α + β (RuleOfLaw_c × ContractInt_i) + γ controls + θ_c + μ_i + ε_ci

eq1 <- feols(ln_exports ~ treat + cap_endow_x_cap_int + skill_endow_x_skill_int |
                           country_code + industry_code,
             data = dt, cluster = ~country_code)

summary(eq1)

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4. IV version using legal origin
# First stage: rule_of_law_c ← legal_origin dummies
# Two‐stage directly in fixest:

eq2 <- feols(ln_exports ~ 1 |                    # no direct regressors besides FE
             .[rule_of_law ~ legal_origin_French +
                             legal_origin_German +
                             legal_origin_Scandinavian +
                             legal_origin_Socialist] *
             contract_intensity +
             cap_endow_x_cap_int + skill_endow_x_skill_int |
             country_code + industry_code,
             data = dt, cluster = ~country_code)

summary(eq2, stage = 1:2)   # show first and second stage

# -------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: alternative outcome—export share in world exports
# Compute world exports per industry
dt[, world_exports := sum(exports_usd), by = industry_code]
dt[, export_share := exports_usd / world_exports]
dt[, ln_share := log(pmax(export_share, 1e-6))]   # avoid log(0)

eq_rob <- feols(ln_share ~ treat + cap_endow_x_cap_int + skill_endow_x_skill_int |
                             country_code + industry_code,
                data = dt, cluster = ~country_code)

etable(eq1, eq2, eq_rob, keep = "treat", fitstat = c("r2","f"))

# End of code
```  

6. Expected Results  
Theory predicts β > 0. A one-standard-deviation increase in RuleOfLaw (≈1 σ ≈ 0.9 index points) should raise exports in a one-SD more contract-intensive industry by roughly 5–10 percent (β ≈ 0.05–0.10 in logs). Given a 2 SD contrast (e.g., 10th vs. 90th percentile institutions), the gap could approach 20 percent.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID with two fixed dimensions)  
C1: Correct counterfactual specified (country & industry FE) … 1  
C2: No major omitted (heterogeneity handled with HO controls) … 0.5  
C3: Parallel trends / exogeneity of interaction term … 0.5  
C4: Correct clustering & inference … 1  
C5: Robustness / falsification exercises implemented … 1  
Overall score: 4 / 5  

─────────────────────────────────────────  
This plan exploits rich cross-country/cross-industry variation, controls for classic Heckscher-Ohlin forces, and tackles endogeneity of judicial quality with historical legal origins, delivering a credible test of whether contract enforcement is a source of comparative advantage.
